extracted.intended_audience: practitioners who practice or seek to practice before the USPTO (patent attorneys/agents, trademark attorneys/agents), law school clinic supervisors, and others interested in OED discipline and practice rules
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, criteria, and program requirements governing practice before the USPTO, Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) processes, signature and supervision requirements, conflicts/informed-consent rules, and examples of disciplinary failures and mitigating/aggravating considerations. Useful for practitioners and clinic supervisors who must comply with USPTO practice and ethics rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Law School Clinic Certification Program (student practice under supervision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allows students in a participating law school’s clinic program to practice before the USPTO under the strict guidance of a law school faculty clinic supervisor; limited recognition for participating students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program permits supervised student practice; supervisors must provide strict guidance. (See: www.uspto.gov/lawschoolclinic.)

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Patent Pro Bono Program (matching under-resourced inventors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent regional programs match financially under-resourced inventors and small businesses with volunteer practitioners to file and prosecute patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors and interested attorneys can find links to regional programs on the USPTO website (www.uspto.gov/probonopatents).

rubrics_metrics.name: OED Diversion Pilot Program — general eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must have willingness and ability to participate in the program; program launched 2017 and extended to 2022.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversion is an alternative to formal discipline; participation requires capability and consent to engage in diversion activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED Diversion Pilot Program — prior discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: In some circumstances, prior discipline is not a bar to diversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior disciplinary history does not automatically disqualify a practitioner from diversion; OED evaluates on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED Diversion Pilot Program — disqualifying misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct at issue must not: involve misappropriation of funds or dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation; result in or be likely to result in substantial prejudice to a client or other person; constitute a 'serious crime' (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.1); be part of a pattern of major similar misconduct or be of the same nature as misconduct for which practitioner has been disciplined within the past five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If misconduct falls into these categories, diversion is inappropriate and formal discipline is more likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice before the Office — scope of activity (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.5(b) & 11.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities that constitute practice before the USPTO include: communicating with and advising a client concerning matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the office (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)); consulting with or giving advice to a client in contemplation of filing a patent application or other document with the office (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1)); consulting with or giving advice to a client in contemplation of filing a trademark application or other document with the office (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners may employ or retain non-practitioner assistants under supervision to assist in matters pending or contemplated before the office. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.14 for who may practice in trademark and non-patent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance definition and initiation of discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.1; § 11.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance: 'a written submission from any source received by the OED Director that presents possible grounds for discipline of a specified practitioner' (37 C.F.R. § 11.1). An investigation may be initiated by receipt of a grievance (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During investigation the OED Director may request information and evidence from: (i) the grievant, (ii) the practitioner, or (iii) any person who may reasonably be expected to provide information and evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible outcomes of OED investigation (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon conclusion of an investigation the OED Director may: close the investigation without issuing a warning or taking disciplinary action; issue a warning to the practitioner; institute formal charges upon approval of the Committee on Discipline; or enter into a settlement agreement with the practitioner and submit it for USPTO Director approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome depends on investigation findings, aggravating/mitigating factors, and Committee approval where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral to Committee on Discipline and timing limits for complaints (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.32, 11.34(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: If investigation reveals grounds for discipline, the matter may be referred to the Committee on Discipline for a probable cause determination (37 C.F.R. § 11.32). Filing timing: complaint must be filed within one year after the date on which the OED Director receives a grievance; no complaint may be filed more than 10 years after the date on which the misconduct occurred (37 C.F.R. § 11.34(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness rules limit when formal complaints can be filed; self-reporting is often considered a mitigating factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline and interim suspension (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.24, 11.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline is based on discipline by a state or federal program or agency and is often conducted on documentary record only (37 C.F.R. § 11.24). Interim suspension may be imposed based on conviction of a serious crime and is referred to a hearing officer for determination of final action (37 C.F.R. § 11.25).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discipline elsewhere or criminal conviction can trigger expedited or documentary proceedings at the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A practitioner shall provide competent representation to a client. Competent representation requires the legal, scientific, and technical knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples (e.g., improper signatures, failing to review specimens, not supervising associates) show lack of competence can lead to suspension or exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must act with diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to file applications, ignoring notices of abandonment, or halting client work without notice are discipline-triggering neglects (see In re Kroll, In re Chirnomas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Client communication and scope of representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.104; § 11.105)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must communicate with clients about the scope of representation, fees, and obtain informed consents when required. 37 C.F.R. § 11.105 addresses communicating scope of representation/fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to notify clients of filing irregularities, improper signatures, or not consulting clients about filings were recurring aggravating factors in cases (e.g., In re Walpert, In re Caraco).

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor toward the tribunal (37 C.F.R. § 11.303)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement; offer evidence known to be false; and in ex parte proceedings must inform the tribunal of all material facts known to the practitioner that will enable the tribunal to make an informed decision, whether or not adverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabricating emails, submitting false declarations, or failing to correct false material facts resulted in exclusion or suspension in cited cases (e.g., In re Walpert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct definitions (37 C.F.R. § 11.804: dishonesty, conduct prejudicial, other)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct includes: (c) dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation; (d) conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice; (i) other conduct adversely reflecting on fitness to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts such as signing clients' names, inserting false features into specifications without client authorization, or paying clients to avoid grievances were treated as serious misconduct (see In re Kroll, In re Starkweather).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest — concurrent conflicts (37 C.F.R. § 11.107)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not represent a client if the representation involves a concurrent conflict of interest. A concurrent conflict exists if (1) representation of one client will be directly adverse to another client; or (2) there is significant risk representation will be materially limited by responsibilities to another client, former client, third person, or by personal interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation despite a concurrent conflict is permitted only if conditions in paragraph (b) are met: (1) practitioner reasonably believes competent and diligent representation can be provided to each affected client; (2) representation not prohibited by law; (3) representation does not involve asserting a claim by one client against another in the same proceeding; and (4) each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing. Case examples (In re Gray, In re Walpert) show failure to manage conflicts leads to exclusion or discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting compensation from third parties (37 C.F.R. § 11.108(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not accept compensation for representing a client from one other than the client unless: (1) the client gives informed consent; (2) no interference with practitioner's independence of professional judgment or with the client-practitioner relationship; and (3) information relating to representation of a client is protected as required by § 11.106.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receiving compensation from third parties without informed consent or permitting third-party direction were repeated problems (see In re Gray, In re Starkweather).

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party payers and control (37 C.F.R. § 11.504(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not permit a person who recommends, employs, or pays the practitioner to render legal services for another to direct or regulate the practitioner's professional judgment in rendering such legal services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing a marketing/referral company to direct filings or application handling resulted in suspension and other discipline (In re Starkweather).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities regarding non-practitioner assistance and supervision (37 C.F.R. § 11.503 and related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners may employ or retain non-practitioner assistants under supervision to assist in matters before the USPTO, but must take reasonable steps to ensure assistants obtain proper signatures and act within permitted roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting non-practitioner assistants to sign, failing to supervise assistants, or failing to retrain staff after discovering improper signatures led to public reprimands, probation, or suspension (In re Sapp, In re Caldwell II, In re Starkweather).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature requirements for trademark filings (37 C.F.R. § 2.193)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each piece of correspondence that requires a signature must bear: (1) a handwritten signature personally signed in permanent ink by the person named as the signatory, or a true copy thereof; or (2) an electronic signature that meets the requirements of paragraph (c) personally entered by the person named as the signatory. Electronic signature requirements include personally entering signature between two forward slashes "/" or using another form specified by the Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing others to enter a practitioner's signature or failing to personally enter required electronic signatures resulted in discipline (multiple cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature requirements for patent filings (37 C.F.R. § 1.4(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Each piece of correspondence requiring a person's signature must: (i) be an original with an original handwritten signature personally signed in permanent dark ink, or (ii) be a direct or indirect copy of an original. S-signature rules: person signing must insert his or her own S-signature. Certification as to the signature is required when using S-signature provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent removal of 37 C.F.R. § 1.4(e) noted; office may require submission of original if authenticity questioned. Improper signature practices can result in exclusion or reprimand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safekeeping client property, fee division, and protecting interests upon termination (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.115, 11.105(e), 11.116)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must properly safekeep client property (e.g., client funds), handle division of fees between practitioners correctly, and protect client's interests on termination of representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commingling client funds, holding client fees in personal accounts, failing to notify clients of abandonment, or improper division of fees were grounds for exclusion (see In re Kroll, In re Chirnomas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to cooperate with disciplinary investigation (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must cooperate with OED investigations; failure to do so is a basis for discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: failure to cooperate led to exclusion on consent in In re Bashtanyk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized practice of law and aiding suspended/excluded practitioners (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(e) / (h))
rubrics_metrics.description: Aiding or permitting a suspended/excluded practitioner to continue practice or assisting unlicensed persons in practice is prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuing to advise clients or draft filings after suspension, even if another registered attorney signs, resulted in exclusion (In re Kroll 2019-15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark 'U.S. counsel' rule (final rule effective Aug. 3, 2019; 84 Fed. Reg. 31498)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign-domiciled trademark applicants, registrants, and parties to TTAB proceedings must be represented at the USPTO by an attorney licensed to practice law in the United States. Canadian patent agents can no longer represent Canadian parties in U.S. TM matters; Canadian TM attorneys/agents may only be additionally appointed practitioners. Clients must appoint U.S.-licensed attorney to file formal responses; USPTO will correspond only with U.S.-licensed attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule eliminates improper foreign representation in U.S. TM matters and requires U.S. counsel in trademark prosecutions and proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating and aggravating factors in discipline (case examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-reporting, full and diligent cooperation with investigation, lack of prior discipline, corrective steps (terminating problematic relationships, retraining staff, informing clients and USPTO) are mitigating; prior disciplinary history, fabricating evidence, paying clients to avoid grievances, and repeated misconduct are aggravating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases illustrate consequences: mitigation can reduce sanction to reprimand/probation; aggravation can lead to multi-year suspension or exclusion (e.g., In re Caldwell II vs In re Kroll).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific misconduct examples treated as sanctionable (case law list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of sanctionable conduct shown in cases: routinely failing to file client applications; posting inventions for sale before filing; entering business relationships with clients without disclosure or informed consent; fabricating emails or evidence; signing clients’ names on USPTO documents; allowing non-practitioners to sign; failing to supervise associates; commingling client funds; failing to pay required filing fees; inserting unauthorized specification changes without client authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each example is linked with rule highlights (competence, diligence, client communication, candor, misrepresentation, safekeeping), and has resulted in public discipline ranging from reprimand to exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hijacking/co-opting of U.S. practitioner data — referral and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances of co-opting/hijacking of U.S. practitioner’s name, address, and/or bar number have occurred; such matters may be referred to state bars and agencies addressing fraud and consumer protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should monitor use of their identifying data; OED may coordinate with other authorities on fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of public discipline decisions (transparency/resource)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions imposing public discipline are available in the FOIA Reading Room and Trademark Official Gazette resources (foiadocuments.uspto.gov/oed/; www.uspto.gov/learning-and-resources/official-gazette/trademark-official-gazette-tmog).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewing published decisions helps practitioners understand enforcement patterns and applicable rules.
